title: The Other Way to the Island
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: Lina ve amcası, göldeki küçük adaya bir gösteri perdesi götürürken kapalı bir köprüyle karşılaşır. Başka bir yol arayışları, haritalara ve yardım istemeye farklı gözle bakmalarını sağlar.
paragraphs: ## The rolled-up sky

Lina carried a roll of blue cloth out of her grandfather's workshop. It was longer than she was tall. Her uncle Sam held the other end. Together, they put it on a small handcart and tied it down with two ropes. The cloth was a screen for a shadow show. That evening, people on Willow Island would see birds, boats, and a large paper moon move across it.

Grandfather came to the door with his walking stick. His ankle still hurt, so he could not go with them. 'Keep it dry,' he said. 'The new paint is ready, but the old wood inside is not very strong.' Lina touched the roll carefully. She had helped him paint the cloth. In the middle was a deep blue sky with tiny white windows for stars.

'We will be there before four,' said Sam. 'The little bridge is only twenty minutes from here.' Grandfather gave Lina a paper map. She laughed. She knew the town well. But he put it in her bag anyway. 'There is more than one way around a lake,' he said. Lina took a bottle of water, some bread, and her phone. Then they set off.

The cart made a soft noise on the street. One wheel was smaller than the other, so it pulled to the right. Lina walked on that side and helped Sam keep it straight. At the bakery, a woman asked about the blue roll. 'We are taking the night sky to an island,' Lina told her. The woman smiled and gave them two small apples for the journey.

Soon they could see the water between the trees. Willow Island stood near the middle of the lake. There was a wooden building on it and a long garden beside it. At the eastern end, a short bridge joined the island to the town park. Lina could already hear someone testing music. They turned the last corner and stopped in front of a red gate.

A sign on the gate said, 'Bridge closed. Please use the western entrance.' Beyond the gate, two workers were lifting a broken wooden board. A branch had fallen onto the bridge during the night. The space under the board looked small, but Sam did not touch the gate. 'We need the other entrance,' he said. Lina looked across the water. The western end of the island was far away.

One worker came over. 'You can go around the north side of the lake,' she said. 'The old farm road goes to the west bridge. It takes about an hour on foot.' She looked at the handcart. 'Perhaps a little longer with that.' Lina thanked her. There was still plenty of time. One hour was not a problem. She opened Grandfather's map on top of the roll.
## A line on the map

The map showed a path beside the water. It went through a garden, past an orchard, and down to the western bridge. Lina followed it with her finger. 'Here,' she said. 'We stay close to the lake.' Sam checked the date in the corner. The map was twelve years old. 'We can start here,' he said, 'but we must read the signs too.'

At first, the path was easy. Ducks moved away from the sound of the cart. A man sat on a bench with three empty fishing buckets. Lina wanted to ask him about the path, but he was asleep. They passed him quietly. A little later, the smooth path became stones. The small wheel hit each stone, and the blue roll moved under its ropes.

They stopped to check the screen. Nothing was broken, but the rope on the left was loose. Lina tied it again. Sam put his jacket between the cloth and the cart. 'The map does not show all these stones,' Lina said. 'Maps are good at lines,' Sam answered. 'They are not always good at wheels.' They pushed on more slowly, choosing the smoothest places.

After ten minutes, they reached the garden on the map. There were neat rows of vegetables behind a low fence. A new greenhouse stood across the old path. A woman was putting small plants into pots. Lina called to her from the gate. 'Excuse me. Is there a way through to the orchard?' The woman put down her pot and came to speak to them.

'The public path moved last year,' she said. 'It goes behind the garden now. You must go back to the white sign.' Lina remembered passing a white sign. She had not read it because she was looking at the map. She felt her face grow warm. Sam only nodded. 'Good. Now we know.' They thanked the woman and turned the heavy cart around.

At the white sign, a narrow path went up a small hill. It looked longer than the old route, but the surface was smooth. Lina folded the map and put it in her pocket. This time, she read every sign. Halfway up, they stopped for water. Through a break in the trees, the island looked smaller than before. They were moving away from it to reach it.

Lina took a photo of the blue roll with the distant island behind it. She sent it to Grandfather with a short message about the closed bridge. His answer came quickly. 'A long entrance for a short show. Thank you both.' Then there was another message. 'Please tell Mira at the island hall. She needs time to hang the screen.' Sam called Mira while Lina held the cart.

Mira answered from a noisy room. She knew about the bridge, but she did not know the screen was still on the road. 'The western bridge is open,' she said. 'Come through the side door when you arrive. And do not hurry on the hill.' Lina liked her calm voice. The show was important, but nobody wanted them to rush with the old wooden frame.
## The orchard gate

The new path ended beside an orchard. Red apples hung above the fence. On the map, the road went straight through the trees. In front of them, however, was another closed gate. There was a bell on a post. Sam rang it. A boy about Lina's age appeared between the trees with a basket in his hands. He looked at the roll. 'A carpet?' he asked.

Lina explained about the screen and the show. The boy's name was Joel. His family looked after the orchard. 'The road through here is private now,' he said. 'There is a public road around the field.' He pointed left. Lina could see it climbing another hill. She tried not to look disappointed. They had already used nearly an hour, and they were not close to the western bridge.

'I can ask my mother about this gate,' Joel added. 'Please wait here.' He went to a low house at the back of the orchard. Lina sat on a flat stone and ate an apple from the bakery. The basket beside the gate was full of much larger apples. Joel returned with his mother. She said they could cross, but a delivery van was using the main track.

'You can take the lower track,' she said. 'Joel will show you. It is flat, but there are some soft places after the rain.' Sam thanked her. Lina offered to pay with their second apple, then saw the trees around her. Joel laughed. 'We have one or two already,' he said. Lina laughed too and put the apple back in her bag.

They followed Joel between the trees. The air smelled of wet leaves and fruit. The track was wide enough for the cart, but Sam kept away from its muddy middle. Joel walked ahead and pointed out the firm ground. For a while, the wheels moved easily. Then the right wheel dropped into a hole under some leaves. The cart stopped so suddenly that Lina almost walked into it.

Sam asked Lina to hold the long roll steady. He and Joel tried to lift the front of the cart. The wheel rose, then sank again. Pulling harder did not help. Lina looked around. Near the fence were some short, flat boards. 'Can we put one under the wheel?' she asked. Joel checked with his mother, who was still close enough to hear. She told him which boards they could use.

They untied the screen and carried it to dry grass first. Without its weight, the cart was easier to lift. Joel slid a board under the wheel. Sam pushed while Lina pulled the handle. This time, the cart came out. There was mud on their shoes and on one rope, but the blue cloth was clean. Lina felt tired and pleased at the same time.

They returned the boards and put the screen back. Joel helped tie both ropes. He showed Lina a knot that was easy to open later. 'A rope must hold,' he said, 'but you do not want to fight it at the end.' Lina tried the knot twice. On her second try, it stayed firm. Sam checked it, and they continued along the orchard track.

At the far gate, Joel stopped. The public road was only a few steps away. Lina invited him and his mother to the show. 'There are birds and boats,' she said. 'And a moon bigger than your basket.' Joel said he would ask. They waved goodbye. The way ahead was clear now, and the western bridge was less than half an hour away.
## Wind above the water

The road ran beside an open field. Without the trees, the wind felt stronger. It pushed against the end of the rolled screen. Sam turned the cart so that the wind came from behind them. Lina held the loose edge of the cloth. Across the field, they could see a stone building and, beyond it, the western bridge. For the first time that afternoon, the island was getting closer.

Then Lina heard a light, sharp sound. One of the ropes had rubbed against a metal corner on the cart. A few thin threads were hanging from it. The rope had not broken, but it was weak. She called to Sam, and they stopped beside the stone building. It was a small café. The sign outside showed a cup and a bicycle.

Inside, the owner was cleaning a table. Sam asked if he had any strong string. The man looked at the cart through the window. 'I have a luggage strap for my bicycle,' he said. 'You can borrow it.' It was green, with a metal buckle. They put it around the screen, away from the sharp corner. Lina wrote the café's name in her phone so they could return it.

The owner brought them two glasses of water. Lina checked the time. It was almost four. They were later than planned, but the show did not start until six. She sent Mira another message. 'At the bicycle café. Coming soon.' Mira replied with a picture of an empty stage. Under it she wrote, 'Your sky has a place waiting.' Lina smiled and showed Sam.

They reached the western bridge just after four. It was a wide bridge with a low wall on each side. A woman in a yellow jacket stood at the entrance. She checked their cart and asked them to walk. Lina had no wish to run. Her arms were tired. As they crossed, she could see the eastern bridge on the other side of the island. It looked very small.

Near the middle, the wind lifted the corner of the blue cloth. Lina caught it with both hands. Nothing came loose. The green strap held the roll firmly. She looked down at the water for a moment, then back at the path. Sam kept both hands on the cart. They crossed the final few metres together and stopped under a large tree on the island.

Mira came out of the hall when she heard the wheels. 'The sky is here!' she called. Two helpers carried the screen inside. Lina followed them through the side door. It opened directly beside the stage. In a few minutes, the long roll was on the floor, the ropes were off, and the blue cloth was opening like a very slow, very large flower.
## A road across the screen

They found one small problem. A wooden ring at the top of the screen was missing. Without it, the middle hung too low. Lina looked at the ropes on the floor. She remembered Joel's knot. With Mira beside her, she made a loop in one clean rope. Mira used it in place of the ring. The screen hung straight. Their long journey had brought a useful lesson with it.

Lina sat near the back while the helpers tested the light. A black paper bird crossed the blue sky. Then a boat sailed past the little white stars. The cloth was not wet or torn. She took a picture and sent it to Grandfather. He called at once. 'It looks beautiful,' he said. Lina told him about the greenhouse, the muddy wheel, and the green strap.

At five thirty, Joel arrived with his mother. The café owner came too, carrying a bicycle helmet. Sam gave back his strap and bought him a cup of tea. Lina saved seats for everyone. She put Grandfather's old map on her knees and drew the new path in pencil. Beside the orchard, she added a little gate. Beside the café, she drew a green line.

Before the show, Mira asked Lina to come to the side of the stage. One helper was ill, and someone needed to move the paper boat. Lina agreed. Behind the screen, she could not see the audience. She could see only the light, the wooden handles, and the waiting shapes. Sam stood nearby. 'A small journey this time,' he whispered. Lina held the boat carefully.

The music started. Lina moved the boat slowly across the blue cloth. A paper hill appeared in its path. She raised the boat around it, then brought it down beside the moon. From the dark room came a child's quiet laugh. Lina thought of the closed bridge and the path behind the garden. Sometimes the best way to a place is the long way round.

After the show, the screen stayed at the hall for another evening. Lina and Sam walked home with an empty cart. The eastern bridge was still closed, so they took the western road again. This time, they knew the turns. Lina's new pencil line was in her pocket. It was not the shortest line on the map, but now she knew every turn of it.

quiz.q: Why is the eastern bridge closed?
options: There is a race on it
quiz.explainTr: Gece düşen bir dal köprüye zarar vermiştir; işçiler kırık tahtayı kaldırmaktadır.

quiz.q: Why must Lina and Sam go back at the garden?
quiz.explainTr: Eski yolun üzerinde artık sera vardır; yeni halka açık yol bahçenin arkasından gider.

quiz.q: What helps them move the cart out of the hole?
quiz.explainTr: Perdeyi indirip arabayı hafifletirler, ardından tekerleğin altına düz bir tahta koyarlar.

quiz.q: What does the café owner lend them?
quiz.explainTr: Kafe sahibi yıpranan ipin yerine kullanmaları için yeşil bir bisiklet kayışı verir.

quiz.q: How does Lina use Joel's lesson at the hall?
options: She makes a rope loop for the screen
quiz.explainTr: Joel'den öğrendiği düğümle temiz ipte bir halka oluşturur; bu halka eksik ahşap halkanın yerini alır.
